header:
Meeting: OnPrem Airgapped runtime / GPU drivers & offline licensing deep dive
Date: 2026-06-12
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 65 minutes
Attendees: Sam Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Tom Nguyen (Helix Head of ML Infra), Erin Walters (Helix Platform Eng), Marco Ruiz (Helix Security), Jenna Park (Helix IT Ops)
summary: Deep technical session focused on on-prem air-gapped delivery: artifact packaging, offline licensing for GPU drivers, runtime installation order, KV cache and batching configuration, quantization tradeoffs for latency vs. throughput. Action items include delivering artifact bundle, scheduling benchmark run, and sharing security/compliance docs.
topics: offline licensing for NVIDIA drivers / GPU firmware
runtime installation order and kernel deps
KV cache behavior and eviction policies
quantization impacts on perf and quality
VPC/on-prem networking considerations for private control plane
transcript:
[00:00] Sam Lee: okay, uh, thanks everyone for joining, we'll kick off. I'm Sam from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Priya, our field SE.
[00:15] Priya Patel: hey all, hi. I'll drive the technical bits, go through the artifact bundle and bench plan.
[00:32] Tom Nguyen: yep thanks, Tom here. Quick context, we're evaluating private deployment inside our co-lo, fully air-gapped, compliance requirements require offline artifacts and signed manifests. We also have to handle offline GPU driver licensing.
[00:50] Erin Walters: and we want to understand the performance tradeoffs — like latency at 1–2 concurrent requests vs throughput for batch scoring.
[01:05] Priya Patel: absolutely, that's the plan. We'll walk through the artifact contents, install order, driver licensing, and then runtime knobs — KV cache, batching windows, quantization profiles.
[01:22] Marco Ruiz: quick security note — Marco from security. We'll need checksums, signed manifests, and an attestation doc. Also, what scope of data leaves the cluster, if any?
[01:35] Priya Patel: no egress by default for Private — control plane can be configured to not call home; for air-gapped we deliver a bundle with a manifest and an offline license for the drivers.
[01:48] Jenna Park: does that bundle include kernel modules or do we rely on the distro repo?
[01:55] Priya Patel: good question. We provide container images and a set of precompiled kernel modules only if customers opt for our kernel-level acceleration package; otherwise we rely on distro-provided drivers. For your air-gapped case, we can include signed driver packages and a step-by-step install script.
[02:10] Tom Nguyen: what's in the artifact bundle, concretely?
[02:18] Priya Patel: tar.gz: runtime containers (optimized inference runtime image), model artifact (optionally quantized weights), optimized kernel patches, driver packages (NVIDIA .run or distro rpm/deb), offline-license token, signed manifest (SHA256), and a small bench harness. We'll also include a README and a verification script that checks signatures.
[02:40] Erin Walters: and how big are these bundles typically?
[02:45] Priya Patel: varies — with a few model variants it can be 20–80 GB. If we include full FP16 weights unquantized it can be larger. We typically recommend bringing the model artifacts separately if size's a concern.
[02:59] Tom Nguyen: on the driver licensing: our procurement requires an offline key that we can hand to our ops team; we can't allow outbound calls to activate. How does Redwood handle that?
[03:12] Sam Lee: we work with the GPU vendor licensing flow — we can provide a signed license file tied to a host fingerprint you provide, or arrange for a one-time activation token that you apply offline. It's part of our offline licensing package.
[03:27] Marco Ruiz: and for verification, we need a chain-of-custody document for the artifacts — who signed what and when.
[03:33] Priya Patel: yes, we include signed manifests and the keys are kept by Redwood's signing service; we can provide the public signing cert for your verification and add timestamps.
[03:45] [04:00] Jenna Park: installation order — driver's first, kernel modules next, then runtime? Any gotchas with CUDA versions?
[04:10] Priya Patel: install drivers and kernel modules first, reboot if kernel updated, then install container runtime (we support containerd/dockerd and have guidance for Singularity), then load our runtime images. CUDA compatibility matrix is in the doc — runtime expects CUDA 12.1 compatible drivers for our latest kernels; older drivers will fall back to a slower path.
[04:35] Tom Nguyen: fallback slower path like 2–3x slower?
[04:40] Priya Patel: depends — for FP16 optimized kernels you'll see bigger gaps. For small batch sizes latency-sensitive workloads the fallback can add 30–80% latency. For large throughput batches it asymptotes closer but still worse.
[04:55] Erin Walters: we care about KV cache behavior — does that persist across requests? eviction policy? memory usage when token counts grow?
[05:10] Priya Patel: KV cache persists in-memory per model version; we have two modes: ephemeral per-request and shared prefix cache. Eviction is LRU with size-based thresholds and configurable TTL. For models with long context we store compressed KV pages and evict at shard level. Memory accounting is exposed in the console and in logs.
[05:30] Tom Nguyen: how about prewarming? can we load common prefixes to reduce first-token latency?
[05:36] Priya Patel: yes, prewarm hooks allow you to prime KV cache for hot prompts; that reduces first-token latency significantly. We typically recommend running a warmup sequence during instance start.
[05:48] [06:00] Erin Walters: batching policies — what's the smallest batching window you support?
[06:06] Priya Patel: we support continuous batching with micro-windows down to 5ms. There's a tradeoff: smaller windows keep latency low at the cost of less batching efficiency. You can configure target latency SLO and the router will dynamically batch up to that SLO.
[06:22] Sam Lee: to add — you can pin routes to dedicated capacity so you don't suffer tail latency from multi-tenant queues.
[06:30] Tom Nguyen: any guidance for throughput numbers on A100 80GB? e.g., tokens/s for 32k context, FP16 vs 4-bit quantized?
[06:42] Priya Patel: ballpark: FP16, 32k context, you might see 100–200 tokens/s single-stream depending on model architecture; with XLA kernels and batching you can push throughput to several thousand tokens/s for batch workloads. With 4-bit quantization (we use q4_0/q4_1 profiles) you often get 1.5–2.5x throughput improvement but quality needs verification. For KV-bound workloads quantization helps memory footprint more than raw compute.
[07:10] Erin Walters: so quantization affects both latency and output quality. How do you validate quality regressions?
[07:17] Priya Patel: we ship evaluation harnesses; you can run your prompt set through FP16 baseline and quantized variants and compare perplexity or task-specific metrics. We also recommend running human evals for sensitive use cases.
[07:30] Tom Nguyen: for the benchmark run, we want to simulate our production distribution — 60% single-request low-latency, 40% bulk scoring. Can the bench harness do mixed workloads?
[07:41] Priya Patel: yes, the harness supports mixed traces, configurable arrival patterns, and will produce latency percentiles and token-level cost estimates. We'll include a guide for mapping your traffic mix.
[07:55] [08:00] Marco Ruiz: a couple of security questions: do any telemetry pings go out by default from the runtime?
[08:07] Priya Patel: no telemetry in air-gapped mode; we disable all outbound by default. The only exception is if you opt into usage reporting and provide a proxy.
[08:18] Marco Ruiz: we also need FIPS-mode crypto for key material operations.
[08:22] Sam Lee: we support FIPS mode for our encryption libs and can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. We'll note that in the security packet.
[08:34] Jenna Park: during installation can your engineer come onsite or do we do it ourselves with instructions?
[08:40] Sam Lee: both. For air-gapped installs we often send a senior SE onsite or do an MSA'ed engagement. For this PoC we can start remote with our step-by-step plus one onsite day if you want.
[08:54] Tom Nguyen: we'd prefer an onsite day for the driver and kernel patch steps.
[09:00] Priya Patel: makes sense. We'll propose a 1-day onsite install then a 2-hour benchmark window the next day.
[09:10] [09:30] Erin Walters: about kernel patches — are these upstream or vendor-specific? Any risk to kernel stability?
[09:37] Priya Patel: the patches we ship are limited to performance-critical paths and are optionally applied; they're tested on mainline and common enterprise distros (RHEL/CentOS/Ubuntu LTS). We always advise staging and can provide a rollback script.
[09:50] Tom Nguyen: can you quantify latency improvements from kernel-level patches?
[09:55] Priya Patel: typical improvements are 5–20% for scheduler and NIC optimizations that benefit tail latency, larger gains for specialized PCIe or NVLink handling depending on workload.
[10:10] Sam Lee: also note that network topology in your co-lo matters: cross-rack latency can add jitter; for low-latency routes we recommend collocating inference GPU nodes and the API gateway.
[10:25] Marco Ruiz: what about licensing constraints for driver redistribution? Some vendors require a signed reseller agreement.
[10:31] Sam Lee: yes, we coordinate with vendors — we include only redistributable packages and the offline license file; for restricted binaries we provide workflow to request a host-bound license from the vendor and we'll facilitate.
[10:44] [11:00] Erin Walters: can you share an example manifest?
[11:05] Priya Patel: yes, sample manifest in the docs — it lists filenames, SHA256 checksums, signing cert fingerprint, intended host fingerprints, and applied flags like "requires-reboot". We'll include an example in the delivery.
[11:20] Tom Nguyen: about host fingerprinting — what inputs do you need?
[11:25] Priya Patel: we can bind license to machine UUID or a TLS client cert fingerprint. For your ops team we usually ask for a short host list and a public key per host.
[11:36] Tom Nguyen: okay. For benchmarking, what metrics will you deliver?
[11:41] Priya Patel: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/s, GPU util, memory usage, KV cache hit rate, batch size distribution, CPU usage, and per-token cost estimate.
[11:53] Erin Walters: for mixed workloads will you provide guidance on batching target windows to meet our 200ms p95?
[11:59] Priya Patel: yes, we'll run knob sweeps to find the batching windows and prefetch settings that meet p95 while maximizing throughput.
[12:12] [12:30] Marco Ruiz: any known gotchas for SELinux/AppArmor?
[12:36] Priya Patel: we have notes — sometimes container runtimes need specific profile adjustments; we can provide ready-made SELinux module snippets to allow our runtime to manage shared memory/pci devices.
[12:48] Jenna Park: shipping physical media — do you provide checksums over the manifest too?
[12:53] Priya Patel: yes, top-level manifest signed and its checksum given out-of-band (PGP or signed email) to ensure chain-of-custody.
[13:04] Tom Nguyen: how long does it take to produce an offline license once we give fingerprints?
[13:09] Sam Lee: usually 24–48 hours, depending on vendor coordination for certain driver packages.
[13:18] [13:30] Erin Walters: about quantization — you mentioned q4_0 and q4_1, what's the difference in practice?
[13:36] Priya Patel: q4_0 is denser packing oriented for max throughput with slightly higher quality regression; q4_1 uses a different scale/zero bias that often yields better quality at a small perf cost. We test both on your prompts.
[13:50] Tom Nguyen: can we get multiple quantized variants in the bundle so we can A/B?
[13:55] Priya Patel: yes, we usually include FP16 baseline + q4_0 + q4_1 and a small script to switch model symlinks for testing.
[14:05] Marco Ruiz: will model weights be encrypted at rest in your packaging?
[14:09] Priya Patel: yes — within the bundle we provide encrypted blobs with a wrap key; the runtime will unwrap using a provided key (or integrate with your HSM). For air-gapped installs we provide the unwrapping key via secure channel.
[14:24] [14:45] Jenna Park: if we use deduped storage across nodes will the runtime handle concurrent access to the KV cache?
[14:52] Priya Patel: KV cache is per-node; we don't yet have a distributed shared KV cache in Private. Deduped storage is fine for model artifacts, but KV cache stays in local RAM/GPU.
[15:05] Tom Nguyen: any recommended monitoring hooks? Prom metrics?
[15:10] Priya Patel: yes, Prom-compatible metrics, logs, and traces — we'll include Grafana dashboards for the common metrics.
[15:20] Sam Lee: quick recap: Redwood will prepare artifact bundle with signed manifest, driver offline license, bench harness, and docs. We'll schedule onsite day plus benchmark window.
[15:36] Tom Nguyen: sounds good. A couple more nitty-gritty: driver versions — can you support our older RHEL7 hosts?
[15:44] Priya Patel: RHEL7 is EOL for some newer drivers; we can support with backported packages but recommend RHEL8/9 for best results. We'll list supported OS matrix in the package.
[15:59] Erin Walters: if we want to run a canary route with dedicated capacity, does that still work in air-gapped Private?
[16:07] Sam Lee: yes — the control plane can be configured to run in your VPC/private control plane; canary routing and rollouts are supported locally. We'll show the config in the docs.
[16:20] [16:40] Marco Ruiz: on the compliance packet, please include data flow diagrams and the audit log retention options.
[16:45] Sam Lee: will do. We'll include audit log retention settings and S3-style retention options for your legal team.
[16:55] Tom Nguyen: any final performance tuning tips?
[17:00] Priya Patel: yes — tune batch sizing to your workload; enable prefix caching for chatty customers; use 4-bit quantization only after running the quality harness; collocate gateway and GPUs; and pin critical routes to dedicated nodes. Also watch for kernel and driver mismatches — they are the most common perf footgun.
[17:20] Erin Walters: ok, let's confirm dates: Sam, you'll send the paperwork and artifact ETA; Priya you'll prepare the bundle; we'll provision hardware and lock an onsite day the week of 6/22.
[17:34] Sam Lee: correct. We'll target sending the package by 6/16 and licensing paperwork by 6/15.
[17:44] Tom Nguyen: thanks everyone.
[17:48] Priya Patel: thanks, we'll follow up with links in the next email.
[18:00] Sam Lee: end call.
